CHAPTER 2 — SIGNS OF LOST CONFIDENCE IN GOD

ON THE EDGE OF THE PROMISE

Israel had come to the border of the Promised Land. Behind them was the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock, and the pillar of cloud and fire. In front of them was the land God had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It was theirs for the taking. Moses reminded them, “Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it, as the LORD God of thy fathers hath said unto thee; fear not, neither be discouraged”(Deuteronomy 1:21). God said, “Possess it.” They said, “Let’s assess it first” (Deuteronomy 1:22). They did not move in faith; they balked in fear. Israel had every reason to trust God, yet once again, they doubted Him.

Faith doesn’t stall; faith steps. Israel had seen enough of God’s power to know that giants didn’t matter. Yet the longer they delayed, the bigger the giants grew and the smaller God seemed in their eyes. Delayed obedience weakens trust, and hesitation strengthens fear. What should have been a day of claiming God’s promise became the starting line of forty years of wandering. (Numbers 13:1–3, Hebrews 10:35–36, Proverbs 3:5–6) How did this happen? How did Israel move to a place of fear after watching God work on their behalf? The answer is simple: they lost confidence in God. When a believer loses confidence in God, there will be warning signs. Israel was no exception. Let’s personally consider these warnings lest we too drift into the wilderness of faithlessness.

REFUSAL TO HEAR

The problem wasn’t that Israel didn’t know what God had said — the problem was they didn’t want to hear it. This wasn’t ignorance; it was deliberate. Moses said, “Notwithstanding ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God: and ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us…” (Deuteronomy 1:26-27). God’s voice was clear, but they tuned it out and turned up the voices of fear. When you refuse the truth, you will believe a lie.

Faith grows when we hear and believe the Word of God (Romans 10:17), but when we plug our ears to God’s promises, fear rushes in to fill the silence. The Israelites heard the truth from Joshua and Caleb, but chose to embrace the hopeless report of the ten spies (Numbers 13:31–33). Refusal to hear is the first step toward the death of confidence in God — because when we stop listening to Him, we start listening to anyone and everything else. (Psalm 81:11–13, Hebrews 3:7–8)

REBELLION AGAINST HIS COMMANDMENTS

Moses didn’t soften the truth: “Ye would not go up, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 1:26). Rebellion isn’t always about shaking a fist at heaven. Sometimes it’s cloaked in what we call “caution” or “wisdom,” but at its heart it still says, “I know better than God.” Rebellion doesn’t just resist God; it reverses direction.

The Israelites even went so far as to talk about choosing a new leader and heading back to Egypt (Numbers 14:4). That wasn’t just fear — it was a complete reversal. God had brought them out to bring them in, and they wanted to go back. Rebellion moves you in the exact opposite direction of God’s blessing. When you choose your way over God’s way, you’re declaring you don’t trust Him. (1 Samuel 15:23, John 14:15)

MURMURING

They didn’t just think these things in their hearts — they “murmured in their tents” against the Lord (Deuteronomy 1:27). Murmuring is unbelief with a voice. It takes God’s blessings for granted, rewrites the past to fit our fears, and spreads like wildfire through the camp. The same people who had walked between walls of water on dry ground now grumbled about how much better it would have been to die in Egypt.

(Psalm 106:24–25, Numbers 11:1)

When praise feels awkward and complaint feels natural, you’re in trouble. Murmuring doesn’t just express dissatisfaction; it multiplies it. The more they spoke it, the more they believed it. It poisoned their perspective until the miracles in their midst were invisible, and their hardships were all they could see. Murmuring is never a small sin — it’s an open declaration that you doubt the goodness of the One who delivered you.

(Philippians 2:14-15, 1 Corinthians 10:10)

DISTORTED VIEW OF GOD

They said, “Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us” (Deuteronomy 1:27). Think about that — the same God who parted the Red Sea, who fed them in the desert, who defeated Pharaoh, they now accuse of hating them. Fear always distorts your view of God.

Growing up in northern lower Michigan, I had many recreational opportunities in the outdoors. I love to hunt and chase whitetail deer both with a bow and a firearm. There are few things more beautiful in life than a crisp October morning in a treestand watching the sun peak over the horizon. I love listening to the chickadees fluttering in the trees, watching the leaves fall all around, and seeing the woods come to life as the morning progresses.

To enjoy this morning view, I have to walk into my spot well before daylight. This can be one of the most

terrifying experiences in the outdoors - especially if your trail camera has shown bears or other predators to be in the area the day before. Trekking through the woods with little to no light is an exhilarating experience. In the dark, everything looks and sounds like a bear, wolf, or the Abominable Snow Monster. My adrenal glands pump over a stump that looks like a critter, a stick that looks like a snake, or the flush of a ruffed grouse that will give any grown man a small heart attack. I have walked these areas hundreds of times in the light with no fear, but without light, it seems more ominous. In the dark, fear causes the beautiful forest to look like a dangerous death trap. Fear distorts reality. Fear always distorts your view of God.

A distorted view of God turns every challenge into proof that He’s against you. Instead of seeing the giants as another opportunity to witness His power, they saw them as evidence of His cruelty. If the enemy can convince you that God is against you, you’ll never take the step of faith that proves He is for you. (Jeremiah 29:11, Romans 8:31–32, Nahum 1:7, Psalm 100:5-25, Numbers 11:1)

SELF-CENTERED CIRCUMSTANCES

They said, “The people is greater and taller than we; the cities are great and walled up to heaven… and there we saw the giants” (Deuteronomy 1:28; Numbers 13:31–33). Notice the focus — greater than we, taller than we, stronger than we. Every measurement was made with man as the standard, not God. When you size up your battles by your strength, the giants will always win.

Self-focus skews perspective. Israel forgot the God who had leveled Egypt with plagues, who had split the Red Sea, who had crushed the mightiest army in the world without a sword raised. Now their eyes were locked on their own weakness instead of His strength. If your gaze is on yourself, your faith will shrink; if your gaze is on God, your faith will grow.

(Psalm 27:1, Isaiah 41:10, 2 Corinthians 12:9)

WORRY AND SELF-PITY

“And all the congregation lifted up their voice, and cried; and the people wept that night. And all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron: and the whole congregation said unto them, Would God that we had died in the land of Egypt! or would God we had died in this wilderness!” (Numbers 14:1–2). Worry imagines the worst. Self-pity believes the worst has already happened. Worry and self-pity don’t just sap courage — they insult the God who has promised His care. Israel forgot that God had never once failed them. The same God who had brought them out of Egypt was able to bring them into Canaan, but worry and self-pity rewrote the story to make God the villain. If the enemy can get you to dwell on your fears long enough, he can make Egypt look better than the Promised Land.

(Matthew 6:25–34, 1 Peter 5:7, Psalm 55:22, Lamentations 3:21–24)

THE OUTCOME

Their unbelief sealed their fate. “But with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness?” (Hebrews 3:17). Unbelief always costs more than obedience. God’s promise didn’t fail — they simply refused to walk into it. Instead of entering the land in days, they wandered in circles for forty years until that generation’s graves marked the desert floor. What they thought was the “safe” choice — avoiding the giants — proved to be the deadliest. They traded milk and honey for manna and funerals. They kept the giants out, but they also kept themselves from God’s best. When you let fear make your decisions, you will always miss the blessings that faith would have claimed.

(Galatians 6:7–8, Proverbs 14:12, Numbers 14:22–23)

THE WAY BACK

The road back to confidence in God isn’t complicated — but it is costly. It demands a heart fully surrendered to Him. Israel had to learn that the same God who led them out was the only One who could lead them in. You can’t get back to confidence IN God without coming back TO God. Coming back to God will require humility, repentance, submission, and remembrance.

Humility – “Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces…” (Numbers 14:5). Humility admits, “Lord, without You I can’t do this.” Pride digs in and defends fear; humility lays it down at the feet of Jesus. You can’t recover confidence in God until you stop pretending you never lost it. (Micah 6:8, James 4:10)

Repentance – Joshua and Caleb stood for truth even when the crowd called for their heads. “Only rebel not ye against the LORD…” (Numbers 14:9). Repentance is more than feeling bad — it’s agreeing with God about your sin and turning from it. It’s choosing His voice over the ten spies EVERY SINGLE TIME. (Acts 3:19, Psalm 51:10) Submission – “…Neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us.” (Numbers 14:9). Submission is bowing to God’s will even when it scares you. You don’t have to understand the path to obey the God who made it. (James 4:7, Proverbs 3:5–6) Obedience does not require explanation.

Rememberance – Finally, remember the Battle is the Lord’s – “If the LORD delight in us, then he will bring us into this land, and give it us.”(Numbers 14:8). Victory isn’t about your strength, your plan, or your resources — it’s about His presence. If He’s with you, that’s all you need. (2 Chronicles 20:15, Exodus 14:14) When God’s people humble themselves, repent, submit, and remember His power, their confidence returns, their steps steady, and they start moving forward again. (2 Chronicles 7:14)

Meditative Thoughts:

• Where have you ASSESSED what God has already told you to POSSESS? (Joshua 1:9)

• Which sign — refusal, rebellion, murmuring, distortion, self-focus, or worry — shows up in you most often? (Psalm 139:23–24)

• What truth about God has FEAR twisted in your mind? (Isaiah 26:3)

• What “giant” looks impossible right now, and how does it look through God’s eyes? (1 Samuel 17:45–47)

• Which step — humility, repentance, submission, or remembering the battle is the Lord’s — do you need to take today? (Philippians 4:13)

CHAPTER 4 — JOSHUA’S ENCOURAGEMENT

A HEAVY ASSIGNMENT

“But Joshua the son of Nun, which standeth before thee, he shall go in thither: encourage him: for he shall cause Israel to inherit it” (Deuteronomy 1:38). God gave Joshua an enormous task—to lead an unleadable people into an unconquerable land. He had seen Moses’ anguish, his grief, his frustration. Joshua knew what it cost to lead Israel. He wasn’t stepping into something easy. He was stepping into something humanly impossible. God knew he would need more than skill or strategy—he would need encouragement.

Encouragement is never a small thing when the task before us is overwhelming. Joshua would face giants, walled cities, and a nation prone to rebellion. Yet God arranged a network of encouragement—divine, spiritual, and personal—to steady him for the road ahead. (Joshua 1:1-5, Psalm 27:1, Hebrews 13:5-6)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD

The first and greatest encourager in Joshua’s life was God Himself. “Now after the death of Moses… the LORD spake unto Joshua” (Joshua 1:1). When God gives an assignment, He never abandons His servant. Joshua didn’t have to invent his mission or fuel his courage alone—God Himself spoke words of strength into his heart. That truth still stands. When you are walking in obedience to God’s will, you can expect His presence, His care, and His encouragement. He is not a distant commander sending you into danger without aid—He is the Captain of your salvation who goes with you into every battle. (Deuteronomy 31:6, Isaiah 41:10, Matthew 28:20)

ENCOURAGED BY MOSES

Moses had been Joshua’s leader, mentor, and commander. From the very beginning, God told Moses: “Encourage him: for he shall cause Israel to inherit it” (Deuteronomy 1:38). Moses had seen Joshua’s faith in the wilderness, and he knew this young man was God’s chosen successor. His charge wasn’t optional—it was essential.

There is no substitute for the peace that comes when a godly leader looks you in the eye and says, “By God’s grace, you can do this.” When I became a new young pastor, I was encouraged by many fellow pastors, servants of God, and church members in a similar way. This instilled such confidence in me. However, I was shocked by how many others “encouraged” me with advice such as, “Just you wait, now you’ll see what it’s really like to be in ministry,” “You’re only 27? Your excitement will wear off soon enough,” and “Oh, the honeymoon will be over soon.” This was obviously not helpful, life-giving, or encouraging. I knew there would be difficulties ahead. I knew there was much I didn’t know and had not experienced, but I was excited to be a pastor! I remind myself often not to “encourage” others in this way. It is not encouraging; it is disheartening. Moses encouraged Joshua by reminding him that the Lord would be with him, and that was all he would need.

Moses, who had endured the murmuring and rebellion of Israel, told Joshua to go forward with confidence. And when Moses laid his hands on him, it was as if God Himself was placing His approval on Joshua’s call. (Numbers 27:18-23, 1 Timothy 4:14)

ENCOURAGED BY ELEAZAR

Joshua also received encouragement from Eleazar the priest. Numbers 27 records that Moses brought Joshua before Eleazar and the congregation to give him a charge in their sight. The high priest would become Joshua’s associate in leadership, a spiritual counselor pointing him toward God’s wisdom and direction.

Encouragement flows not only from God and from leaders but also from spiritual mentors who walk beside us. Eleazar’s presence reminded Joshua that he was not leading alone. God had provided godly counsel, spiritual reinforcement, and intercession. Joshua was encouraged by prophet, priest, and king - Moses, Eleazar, and God. The same is true for us: God often places encouragers in our path if we are humble enough to listen. (Proverbs 11:14, Hebrews 13:17)

ENCOURAGED BY VICTORIES

One of the ways God strengthened Joshua was by reminding him of what he had already seen. He had stood on the battlefield when Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, fell. “Thine eyes have seen all that the LORD your God hath done… so shall the LORD do” (Deuteronomy 3:21).

When the future looks impossible, look back at God’s past faithfulness. Joshua’s encouragement wasn’t only in the promise of what God would do—it was in the memory of what God had already done. Every past victory was a pledge of future triumph. (1 Samuel 17:37, Psalm 77:11-12, Philippians 1:6)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD’S PRESENCE

Joshua was told again and again: “The LORD your God he shall fight for you” (Deuteronomy 3:22). When God sends you into battle, He does not leave you to fight alone. His presence is both the guarantee of victory and the cure for fear.

David would later stand before Goliath with the same confidence, declaring that the battle is the Lord’s. Joshua could march forward with courage, not because he was mighty, but because his God was. And the same God who fought for Joshua fights for His children today. (Exodus 14:14, 1 Samuel 17:47, Romans 8:31)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD’S PROMISES

God’s promise of the land was not new—it stretched back to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But now it was Joshua’s turn to believe it personally. Moses was told: “Charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people” (Deuteronomy 3:28). God’s promises are never “if” but “when.” Joshua’s encouragement was anchored in the certainty of God’s Word. What God has spoken, He would do. Faith finds its courage not in what we see but in what He has said. (Romans 4:20-21, 2 Corinthians 1:20, Hebrews 10:23)

ENCOURAGED BY SONGS

Moses even left behind a song to be sung in Israel as a witness (Deuteronomy 32). Deuteronomy 31 tells us that God commanded Moses to teach it to the people so that when trouble came, the melody of truth would echo in their hearts.

Songs have a unique way of carrying truth into the soul. They remind us of God’s character, His works, and His promises. That’s why Scripture tells us to speak to ourselves “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.” Joshua’s encouragement included not only commands and victories but also songs of faith that would outlast the darkest days. (Ephesians 5:19, Colossians 3:16, Psalm 42:8)

ENCOURAGED BY WISDOM

After Moses’ death, the people wept for thirty days, asking, “What are we going to do without Moses?” But the Lord had already provided. “And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him” (Deuteronomy 34:9).

God never leaves His people leaderless or powerless. Joshua’s encouragement was in knowing that God had given him divine wisdom for the task. That same wisdom is offered freely to every believer who asks in faith. (James 1:5, Isaiah 11:2, Colossians 1:9)

ENCOURAGED BY GOD’S PROSPERITY

When Joshua finally stepped into leadership, God gave him this promise: “Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you” (Joshua 1:3). No enemy, no obstacle, no limitation could stand in the way of God’s plan.

Encouragement comes when we realize that success in God’s work is not based on our ability but on His faithfulness. Yielded hearts, Spirit-filled lives, and obedient steps will always find the path open and the victory sure. (Joshua 1:5, Proverbs 16:3, Romans 8:37)

JOSHUA’S QUIET CONFIDENCE

Joshua didn’t seize leadership with fanfare. He simply issued a calm directive: “Prepare you victuals; for within three days ye shall pass over this Jordan” (Joshua 1:11). No drama. No delay. Just steady faith in God. Joshua was ready to move with God, and because of his encouragement in the Lord, he did in a few days what Moses could not in forty years. Encouragement turns fearful hesitation into faithful action. (Psalm 31:24, Isaiah 40:31, 2 Timothy 1:7)

Meditative Thoughts:

• Who has God placed in your life to encourage you? How have you responded to their words? (Proverbs 27:17)

• What past victories can you remember that should fuel your faith for today? (Psalm 77:11)

• Are you fighting in your own strength, or resting in the

Lord’s presence and power? (Zechariah 4:6)

• Which promise of God do you need to claim with fresh courage right now? (Hebrews 10:23)

• Are you encouraging the next generation to step into

God’s call with confidence? (2 Timothy 2:2)
